title: The shape of a distribution: skewness and kurtosis

videos.script: Centre and spread are two numbers. Data has a shape as well, and the shape can change what those two numbers mean. {{shape}} Draw a histogram of Horta's baskets. Most of them pile up between forty and eighty reais, and then a thin tail stretches far to the right. That is a skewed shape. {{skewed}} Draw the weights of bags of rice from a filling machine. They pile up around one kilogram and fall away evenly on both sides. That is symmetric. {{symmetric}} Now draw the times of day when people order. Two piles. One at lunch, one at dinner, and an empty afternoon between them. The mean lands at six minutes past four, when almost nobody orders. {{bimodal}} This lesson gives these shapes names, and two numbers that measure them. Skewness says which way the tail runs. Kurtosis says how heavy the tails are. {{numbers}} And it starts with a warning about the histogram itself, because the same data can be drawn to look like three different things. {{warning}}
